question: What are the two primary cell types that make up nervous tissue?
explanation: Nervous tissue is composed of excitable neurons that transmit electrical signals and supportive neuroglia that protect and nourish them. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h1)

question: Which nervous system function involves the processing and interpretation of sensory input?
explanation: Integration occurs within the central nervous system where incoming sensory information is analyzed to formulate a suitable response. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h1)

question: What is the primary function of dendrites on a neuron?

options.A: Insulating the axon against signal loss

explanation: Dendrites act as receptive areas that collect incoming electrochemical signals and conduct them toward the cell body. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h2)

question: Where is the trigger zone typically located on a standard multipolar neuron?
explanation: The axon hillock is the specialized region where graded potentials are summed and action potentials are initiated. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h2)

question: Which structural class of neurons is most commonly found throughout the human nervous system?
explanation: Multipolar neurons have multiple dendrites and a single axon, making up the vast majority of neurons in the brain, spinal cord, and motor pathways. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h3)

question: A patient touches a hot stove and immediately pulls their hand back. What functional class of neuron carries the signal from the spinal cord to the skeletal muscles of the arm?
explanation: Motor or efferent neurons carry commands away from the central nervous system out to peripheral effectors like skeletal muscles. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h3)

question: Which glial cell type is responsible for forming the myelin sheath in the peripheral nervous system?
explanation: Schwann cells wrap around peripheral nerve fibers to create the insulating myelin sheath, unlike oligodendrocytes which perform this role in the central nervous system. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h4)

question: Which of the following cells acts as a resident immune cell and phagocyte within the central nervous system?
explanation: Microglia monitor neural health and transform into active phagocytes to clear cellular debris and infectious agents from central nervous tissue. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h4)

question: What name is given to the periodic gaps in the myelin sheath along an axon?
explanation: Nodes of Ranvier are exposed areas along a myelinated axon where voltage-gated ion channels cluster to facilitate saltatory conduction. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h5)

question: Why is saltatory conduction faster than continuous conduction?

options.A: Neurotransmitters are released directly into the myelin sheath to speed up travel time.
options.B: Unmyelinated fibers lack potassium channels required for repolarization phases.
options.C: Myelin actively pumps sodium ions out of the axon at a much higher metabolic rate.
options.D: Action potentials jump from node to node rather than traveling continuously along the entire membrane.

explanation: By skipping the myelinated segments and regenerating only at the nodes of Ranvier, electrical signals travel much more rapidly down the axon. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h5)

question: What is the approximate resting membrane potential value of a typical unstimulated neuron?
explanation: A resting neuron maintains an intracellular charge of about -70 millivolts relative to the outside environment. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h6)

question: What physiological event characterizes the depolarization phase of an action potential?

options.B: Outflow of potassium ions from the cell
options.C: Active pumping of calcium ions into vesicles
options.D: Inflow of sodium ions into the cell

explanation: Depolarization occurs when voltage-gated sodium channels open, allowing positively charged sodium ions to rush down their gradient into the neuron. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h6)

question: Which ion influx at the axon terminal directly triggers the exocytosis of synaptic vesicles?
explanation: The arrival of an action potential opens voltage-gated calcium channels at the axon terminal, prompting vesicles to fuse with the membrane and release neurotransmitters. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h7)

question: What prevents continuous, unending stimulation of the postsynaptic cell by lingering neurotransmitters?

options.A: Permanent closure of the presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels
options.B: Immediate destruction of the postsynaptic receptor proteins by lysosomes
options.C: Enzymatic degradation or cellular reuptake in the synaptic cleft
options.D: Reversal of the action potential back toward the axon hillock

explanation: Signaling is halted when neurotransmitters are either broken down by enzymes or actively cleared from the cleft via reuptake mechanisms. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h7)

question: What primary factor prevents extensive axonal regeneration in the central nervous system?

options.A: Instant destruction of neuronal cell bodies throughout the brain
options.B: A complete absence of microglial cells to clear debris
options.C: Glial scar formation and growth-inhibiting factors from oligodendrocytes
options.D: Rapid overproduction of acetylcholine in the synaptic clefts

explanation: Astrocytic scars and inhibitory proteins produced by oligodendrocytes create a hostile environment that blocks axonal regrowth in the central nervous system. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h8)

question: What is the role of Schwann cells during the repair of a damaged peripheral nerve fiber?

options.A: Synthesizing new myelin to prevent Wallerian degeneration
options.B: Forming a regeneration tube to guide the growing axon sprout
options.C: Releasing excitatory toxins to eliminate damaged dendrites
options.D: Converting into astrocytes to bridge the central nervous gap

explanation: Peripheral Schwann cells proliferate and align to form a conduit or regeneration tube that directs the regenerating axonal tip back to its target. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h8)
